Two teams collected thousands of labelled examples: a team trained analysts to label real transactions, and a team wrote mock transactions with known patterns. Every explanation starts from scratch each time, so there is no hidden inside information.

By default the Explorer shows the template. When the data is too unusual to fit a template, the Explorer chooses the simplest explanation: the transaction is not flagged. In other words, when the answer is not obvious, the choice stays within the range the data was trained on.
All times are in UTC, taken from the block that confirmed the transaction.

The first line says whether the method flagged the transaction: "Yes" if so, and "No" if not. Then each reason names a feature, says how this transaction compares with the address's usual value, and gives both values. Start with the first reason: it is the strongest. The original plan used 3.5, but on our data that left 7 addresses with more than 20% of their transactions flagged. No threshold we tested brought every address under that limit. 5 left the fewest (4) while still finding at least 70% of 2 of the 3 planted patterns, so the team chose it. The decision and its evidence are recorded in the change log.

Two public labelled datasets: Elliptic, Bitcoin transactions labelled by the dataset's authors, and Elliptic2, their re-labelled version. We use them to train and test classifiers with accuracy, precision, recall and F1, and to check how far unusual coincides with their labels. They are never used to label the Explorer's addresses.

Our unusualness methods ranked the labelled positive transactions below chance on both datasets, while a classifier trained on the labels did far better. In other words, labelled activity often looks typical. That is why the Explorer only ever says unusual.

When one method flags a transaction and the other does not, we use the flag. If both do, we look at the addresses' activity around that time and flag if it seems unusual then. Scores are never combined; the strongest signal is used.

Drift happens when an address is very regular for a while and then becomes very irregular, such as suddenly moving far from its usual value. The Explorer flags it because the change is so extreme; the underlying reason, such as a one-time event, is not diagnosed.

Two public labelled datasets: Elliptic, BitcoinHeist and Elliptic2. Our methods found the most planted patterns on each, and on a held-out test collection from Elliptic they found the most planted patterns too. One of them, ScoreF, was the baseline: a classifier with accurate features but no pattern-finding; the others, TxGPT2 and TxRNN, found patterns by training from scratch.

It means no single feature is far from usual: the address's behaviour has not changed. That is still worth a look, though: an address usually becomes unusual when one feature moves away from usual, and unusual activity requires investigation, while ordinary variation does not.

Bitcoin amounts and gaps are extremely skewed: a handful of huge transactions would pull an average and a standard deviation far away from typical activity. The median and the median absolute deviation ignore those few extremes, so the usual value stays usual.

Esplora collects 20 addresses with long histories and 20 with short ones, from at least 20 different wallets. A teammate writes down the reason for each flag, and we check that against the code. One reason: a flag measures difference from the past, and ordinary events cause differences too. The reasons show how the flags line up with ordinary variation, so you can read them out loud.

It varies by address. Most addresses have few flags, but an address whose behaviour changed, for example one that became much busier, can have many in that period. A run of flags usually means the address changed its pattern, which is itself worth a look.

With each new block the Explorer's scoring uses the address's earlier history, so an address can become uncatchy after a run of catches. That is what the test collection measures: how far behind the frontier the methods look.
With the Explorer's chosen method, a transaction is flagged when at least one feature has a robust z of 5 or more in absolute value. Features from 2 upward are listed as contributing reasons.

Two public labelled datasets: Elliptic, BitcoinHeist and Elliptic2. Two independent checks: every method was tested on the other set. Every method was tested with both kinds of scoring, and every score used every method. The Explorer shows the best found, leaves the choice open.

We planted synthetic transactions with known patterns into real histories and measured how many each method found: a spike (10 times the usual amount), a burst (10 transactions within 24 hours) and a dormancy (60 to 120 days of silence). Real transactions have no labels, so we never claim accuracy on them.

Isolation Forest builds many random trees that split transactions apart. Unusual transactions are isolated after only a few splits. The Explorer flags the top 2% of scores seen during training.

TxGPT learned from thousands of other address histories collected for training, with the addresses stored only as salted hashes. The addresses the Explorer shows were excluded, so it never scores an address it was trained on.

TxGPT is a small language model trained from scratch on transaction sequences instead of words: each transaction becomes tokens for its gap, direction, amount, inputs, outputs and fee. Its surprisal measures how unexpected a transaction is given everything before it, and it can say which part was surprising.
With the Explorer's chosen method, one of the previous 30 days is used. A different period can be specified as an option.

Every reason ends with "Unusual", but that does not mean the transaction is. A flag is a signal to look at the transaction; it is not a verdict. Unusual activity requires investigation; it does not indicate wrongdoing.
Gap (F3) means the gap between this transaction and the one before it is unusually long: 24 hours or more. That is all. The Explorer's flag says no; the reason gives a reason.

With the Explorer's chosen method, a week with very few transactions is almost never flagged: the limit is 20% below the usual amount, and addresses often have much less in the same direction. When we do flag a week, it is almost always because the amount is far below what the address usually moves, and the shape of the countline is very different from usual.

By default the Explorer shows the template. When the Assistant is switched on, two models can rephrase it. A pretrained 3-billion-parameter model writes first where a GPU is available and also answers general questions, and a 152-million-parameter model writes next. Both go through the same checks, and the template is the final fallback.

Investigations often start from activity that departs from an established pattern, for example a wallet suddenly moving far more than usual. The Explorer surfaces those departures quickly and explains them, so a person can decide what deserves attention.
Size (F1) means the amount of the transaction was close to the address's usual amount in the same direction. For example, if an address was usually very active, a small withdrawal would be unusual.
The Explorer shows a Bitcoin address's transaction history and ranks each transaction by how unusual it is compared with that same address's own past.

With the Explorer's chosen method, an address is compared only with itself, so it gives the most precise picture. When an address is very busy, its spread can be almost zero, and any tiny change would look enormous. The Explorer therefore uses a fixed baseline when the address is very busy, so that spreads are shown in the same unit.

DBSCAN finds dense groups of similar points and labels the rest. Points in different groups can be scattered far apart. DBSCAN does not order points by distance, so the distance to the next nearest neighbour is usually longer than the shortest one.

Relative size (F1) divides this amount by the address's usual amount in the same direction, so 10x means ten times the usual. The explanation compares that ratio with the ratio the address usually has, so a higher ratio than usual can still be below 1x when the address's ratios are usually even lower.

Regression models predict the size of a transaction a user is likely to receive, given the direction and amount they just sent. One of them is used as a proxy for the expected amount of the next transaction in the same direction, and the ratio to that amount is compared with the ratio the address usually has.

No. A flag only means something stands out from the address's past: larger, faster, busier or differently shaped than usual. There are many ordinary reasons for that, such as a one-off purchase or a change of wallet software. Unusual activity requires investigation; it does not indicate wrongdoing.

Nine methods score every transaction: the robust-z baseline; regression of the expected size and gap, used two ways (how far off the prediction is, and whether it falls outside a calibrated expected range); K-Means distance; DBSCAN noise; Isolation Forest; Local Outlier Factor; TxGPT, a small language model of transaction sequences; TxRNN, a small recurrent neural network; and TxLSTM, a small long-memory recurrent neural network. The Explorer shows one of them by default: the robust-z baseline.
Local Outlier Factor compares how crowded each transaction's neighbourhood is with the average neighbourhood radius. A transaction in a much sparser spot than usual is unusual.

By the Explorer's Rule: every explanation starts from scratch each time an address is scored, so it cannot depend on what it scored before. The main reasons an explanation is found are a robust z of 5 or more on one feature, or 3 or more on each of two features; below that the address is not labelled.

With only a few transactions on record, any one of them can seem like an outlier. That is why the Explorer only ever says an address is unusual when at least 20 earlier transactions are recorded. Before that, the earlier history is too short to compare against.

Many inputs means the transaction assembled itself from several earlier coins, rather than starting from scratch. That is unusual for an address's own transactions, but on its own it says nothing about the address's behaviour.

A burst (F1) is when an address is busier than usual: much more activity in one direction than the address usually has. For example, if an address is normally quiet but suddenly moves thousands of satoshis at once, that would be a burst. A burst can still happen within a normal week of activity; it just means the activity happened much faster than usual.

The Explorer uses nine features: amount, direction, time of day, week of year, gap, shape, flatness, kurtosis and skewness. Each one can be zero or more, and the reasons list them out. The z numbers measure how far apart a feature is from the usual value: a positive number means above usual, a negative number means below usual. The first few reasons list the features with the strongest differences, so if you scroll past them the z numbers no longer mean very different things.

K-Means groups transactions into a few typical patterns. Each group, or "cluster," has many transactions in common. The Explorer finds the best way to divide a transaction's features into those few patterns.

It means the method flagged the transaction: one of the nine features, taken two at a time, has a robust z of 5 or more in absolute value. That is the most sensitive part of the test, and flags deserve scrutiny. The judgement is not wrong, but it is close: a flag is a reason to look, not a conclusion.
